mainTopic: How the wording of a sale decides what is sold: outer boundaries (מצרים) that are only a broad description, the clause 'I held back nothing', and what words like ארעא, ארעתא and זיהרא include.
overview: The גמרא explains that the משנה's rule (a room behind the house is not sold with it) holds even when the seller listed boundaries outside that room. It supports this with רב נחמן in the name of רבה בר אבוה: a seller who sells one residence in a big בירה and lists the building's outer boundaries has only described the location broadly. The גמרא asks what case this covers and answers with a mixed place, where people use the words in different ways. Since the seller did not write 'I have not held back anything', he clearly kept something back. רב נחמן gives the same ruling for a field inside a large בקעה, with the same question and answer. The גמרא then explains why both rulings were needed, since each case has a feature the other lacks. It shows that אביי's advice to always write 'I have not held back anything' follows רב נחמן. Finally, through רב אשי's case of two plots called 'בי חייא' and a list of sale wordings, the גמרא shows how much each wording covers: 'land' is one plot, 'lands' is two, 'all lands' is every field but not orchards, and 'זיהרא' takes in orchards too but not houses or slaves.

steps.title: Even when outer boundaries were listed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the משנה's rule is needed for a case where the seller listed boundaries outside the room.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the rule is needed for a case where the seller described the boundaries using markers outside that room.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is answering an earlier question about why the משנה needed to say that the inner room is not sold. It says the rule teaches something new: even if the seller's document listed boundaries that seem to include that room.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without this, we might think that listing outer boundaries proves the room was included. The משנה tells us that is not so. The room is still not part of the sale.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for (the case where...)

phrases.english: No, it is necessary,
for even though he marked out the boundaries for him
with boundaries on the outside –
phrases.notes: He means boundaries outside the room behind the house, so on paper the room looks like it is inside the sale.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, דְּאַף עַל גַּב דִּמְצַר לֵיהּ מִצְרֵי אַבָּרַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from before this section about why the משנה's rule was needed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case: the rule applies even with outer boundaries listed.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Listing outer boundaries would include the inner room in the sale.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even with outer boundaries listed, the inner room is not sold.

steps.title: רב נחמן: wide boundaries are only a general description
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן, in the name of רבה בר אבוה, rules that a seller who lists a big building's outer boundaries has only sold the one residence.
steps.simpleTranslation: This follows רב נחמן, who said in the name of רבה בר אבוה: if someone sells a residence inside a large building and lists the building's outer boundaries, he only described the boundaries broadly.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a source for the idea in step 1. רב נחמן teaches that listing wide boundaries does not widen the sale itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The seller sold one residence. He used the big building's edges only as a general way to say where it is. The boundaries were 'stretched' for description, not for ownership.

keyTerms.meaning: A residence or house (here, one unit)
A large building holding several residences

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the key principle: boundaries written in a sale document can be a loose description. They do not always define exactly what is sold.

phrases.english: In accordance with Rav Naḥman,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ:
phrases.english: as Rav Naḥman said in the name of Rabba bar Avuh:
One who sells a residence to his fellow
within a large building,
even though he marked out for him
the outer boundaries –
he merely widened the boundaries for him.
phrases.notes: In other words, the seller described the location loosely. He did not hand over the whole building.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּדְרַב נַחְמָן, דְּאָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source principle behind step 1's answer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Listing a large building's outer boundaries when selling one residence in it only describes the location. The rest of the building is not sold.

steps.title: What case is רב נחמן talking about?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the exact case. If people clearly separate the words בית and בירה, the ruling is obvious.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If people call a residence a 'residence' and a building a 'building', this is obvious: he sold a residence, not a building!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now questions רב נחמן's ruling. It tries the first possible case and shows that it makes the ruling too obvious to need saying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the seller's words clearly mean one residence, nobody would think he sold the whole building. So רב נחמן must be teaching about some other case.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What are the circumstances?

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?
If we say that they call a residence a 'residence'
and a building a 'building',
it is obvious –
he sold him a residence,
he did not sell him a building!

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָמֵי? אִילֵּימָא דְּקָרוּ לֵיהּ לְבַיִת ״בַּיִת״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions what case step 2's ruling covers.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: In what kind of place, based on how people use the words, does רב נחמן's ruling apply?
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Where the words are clearly separate, the ruling is too obvious to need teaching.

steps.title: If a building is also called a residence, all was sold
steps.stepSummary: The second possible case fails the other way. If people also call a בירה a בית, the whole building should be sold.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, perhaps they also call a building a 'residence'? Then he sold him all of it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the second possible case. It shows that here רב נחמן's ruling would seem wrong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the word 'בית' can mean the whole building, and the outer boundaries match the whole building, the sale should cover everything. Now both possible cases seem to fail.

phrases.english: Rather, where they also call a building a 'residence'?
Then he sold him all of it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the two-sided challenge that step 3 began.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Here the word בית plus the outer boundaries would point to selling the entire building, which goes against רב נחמן.

steps.title: A mixed place where most people separate the words
steps.stepSummary: The answer: רב נחמן speaks of a place where most people separate בית from בירה, but some people call a בירה a בית.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it is needed where most people call a residence a 'residence' and a building a 'building', but some also call a building a 'residence'. You might have said he sold all of it, so רב נחמן teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by finding a middle case. In that case the ruling is neither obvious nor wrong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since some people use 'בית' for the whole building, and the outer boundaries were listed, we might think the whole building was sold. רב נחמן teaches that it was not, and the next step gives the reason.

phrases.english: No, it is necessary
where most people call a residence a 'residence'
and a building a 'building',
but there are also some who call a building a 'residence';
you might have said he sold him all of it,
so he teaches us otherwise –

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, דְּרוּבָּא קָרוּ לֵיהּ לְבַיִת ״בַּיִת״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the two-sided challenge of steps 3–4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A middle case: mixed use of the words
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since some call a בירה a בית and the outer boundaries were listed, the whole building was sold.

steps.title: The missing clause shows he held something back
steps.stepSummary: The proof: the seller did not write 'I have not held back anything in this sale', which shows he did hold something back.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he meant to sell everything, he should have written 'I have not held back anything in this sale'. He did not write it, so we learn that he held something back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the reason behind רב נחמן's ruling in the mixed case. This completes the answer about the house and the building, and the next step brings a parallel ruling about a field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A seller who sells everything normally writes a clause saying he kept nothing. Leaving that clause out shows he kept part of the building. So the wide boundaries were only a description.
steps.whatToRemember: Listing wide outer boundaries does not widen a sale. Unless the seller writes that he held nothing back, we assume he only sold what he named: the residence, not the whole building, and the house, not the room behind it.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the outer boundaries decide what was sold. The deciding point is the missing clause 'I have not held back anything'. Without it, the seller kept the rest.

phrases.english: since he should have written:
'And I have not held back anything in this sale',
and he did not write it,
learn from this that he did hold something back.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִדַּהֲוָה לֵיהּ לְמִכְתַּב: ״וְלָא שַׁיַּירִית בִּזְבִינִי אִלֵּין כְּלוּם״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reason for the answer in step 5.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Leaving out the clause 'I have not held back anything' shows the seller kept the rest. The listed boundaries are only a broad description.

steps.title: Selling a field inside a big valley
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן in the name of רבה בר אבוה rules that a seller who lists the outer boundaries of a big valley has only sold the one field. He simply described the boundaries broadly.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב נחמן said in the name of רבה בר אבוה: If someone sells a field to his friend inside a big valley, even if he listed the outer boundaries of the whole valley, he just described the boundaries broadly. He only sold the one field.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second ruling from the same רב נחמן, built just like the בית and בירה ruling, but now about a field inside a big valley.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The seller wrote the borders of the whole בקעה, but he only sold one שדה inside it. The wide borders only tell the buyer where the field is located. They do not mark exactly what was sold.

keyTerms.meaning: A large valley, a wide stretch made up of many fields
He widened the borders for him, describing them broadly

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ:
phrases.english: And Rav Naḥman said in the name of Rabba bar Avuh:
One who sells a field to his friend
in a large valley of fields,
even though he marked out for him
the outer boundaries,
he just made the boundaries wide for him.
phrases.notes: He means the seller only gave a broad location. He did not sell everything inside those lines.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel ruling by the same rabbis, moving from a building to a field.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Listing a בקעה's outer boundaries sells only the one field. The boundaries were just a broad description.

steps.title: What is the case? If the words are kept apart, it is obvious
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the exact case. If everyone clearly separates שדה from בקעה, the ruling seems too obvious to need saying.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If you say it is a place where people call a field a 'field' and a valley a 'valley,' then it is obvious: he sold him a field, not a valley!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries to pin down the case for רב נחמן's ruling. It starts by testing the first possibility.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the local language always keeps שדה and בקעה apart, then a contract that says 'field' plainly means one field. Then רב נחמן would be teaching nothing new. This is the same pattern the גמרא used for בית and בירה.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What are the exact circumstances?

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?
If you say that they call a field a 'field'
and a valley a 'valley',
it is obvious:
he sold him a field,
he did not sell him a valley!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the exact setting of the ruling in step 7.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: In what language setting does רב נחמן's field ruling apply?

steps.title: If a valley is also called a field, everything should be sold
steps.stepSummary: The second possible case fails the other way. If people also call a בקעה a שדה, the whole valley should be sold.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say it is where people also call a valley a 'field.' Then he sold him the whole thing!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries the opposite case and shows that it leads to the opposite ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'field' can mean the whole valley, then the word 'field' together with the outer boundaries points to selling all of it. That goes against רב נחמן. So neither simple case fits his ruling.

phrases.english: Rather, where they also call a valley a 'field'?
Then he sold him all of it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the first case is rejected as obvious, this rejects the second case as leading to the opposite ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's ruling that only the field is sold
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the word 'field' covers the valley, the outer boundaries plus the word 'field' should sell the entire valley.

steps.title: The case: a place with mixed usage
steps.stepSummary: The answer is that רב נחמן speaks of a place where some people separate the words, but others call a בקעה a שדה. We might have thought the whole valley was sold.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the ruling is needed where some people call a field a 'field' and a valley a 'valley,' but there are also some who call a valley a 'field.' You might have said he sold him all of it, so רב נחמן teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by naming a middle case: a place where people use the word 'field' in mixed ways.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the word 'field' could go either way here, the wide boundaries might seem to prove that the whole valley was sold. רב נחמן teaches that this is not so. The reason is explained in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for this case

phrases.english: No, it is needed
where there are some who call a field a 'field'
and a valley a 'valley',
and there are also some who call a valley a 'field';
you might have said he sold him all of it,
so he teaches us:

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, דְּאִיכָּא דִּלְשָׂדֶה קָרוּ לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves both rejected cases by picking a middle setting.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defines a middle case between the two rejected options
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since 'field' might mean the valley, the outer boundaries show the whole valley was sold.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only the one field is sold, even in a place with mixed usage.

steps.title: Proof: he never wrote 'I held back nothing'
steps.stepSummary: The seller did not write 'I have not held back anything in this sale.' That shows he did hold something back.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since he could have written for him, 'I have not held back anything in this sale,' and he did not write it, learn from this that he did hold something back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the reason for רב נחמן's teaching. A missing sentence in the contract shows what the seller meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A seller who really wants to sell everything inside the borders can say so with a standard sentence. Leaving that sentence out shows he kept part of the valley. This is the same reasoning used in the בית and בירה case.

keyTerms.meaning: I did not hold back anything

steps.whatToRemember: With both a building and a valley, wide boundaries do not sell everything inside them unless the seller writes 'I held back nothing.'

phrases.english: Since he should have written for him:
'I have not held back for myself anything in this sale',
and he did not write it for him,
learn from this that he did hold something back.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the reason behind the קא משמע לן of step 10.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Leaving out the clause 'I held back nothing' shows the seller kept part of the valley, so only the field is sold.

steps.title: Why both rulings were needed: the house case alone was not enough
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains why רב נחמן taught both rulings. From the house alone, we might think a בקעה, which has one single use, is sold whole.
steps.simpleTranslation: And both rulings are needed. If he had taught us only about the house, we might say that is because the residence has its own use and the building has its own use. But a valley is all used one way, so we might say he sold him all of it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers an unspoken question: why did רב נחמן need to say both rulings, when they look the same? It begins with why the field ruling adds something beyond the house ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The residence has its own separate use, apart from the rest of the big building, so it is easy to see them as separate. A valley is all farmland used the same way, so we might think one sale covers all of it. That is why the field ruling had to be said too. The other half, why the house ruling was needed, comes next.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think this step disagrees with רב נחמן. It only explains why he had to teach the field case separately. The ruling stays the same: only one field is sold.

phrases.english: And it is necessary to teach both;
for if he had taught us only the house,
that is because this one has its own use
and that one has its own use,
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the residence and 'that one' is the big building around it.

phrases.english: but a valley,
which is all one single use,
I would say he sold him all of it;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After both rulings are explained, the גמרא shows why each one was needed, starting with the field ruling.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The field ruling was needed because a valley's single use might suggest it is sold whole. The house case alone would not teach that.

steps.title: Why the valley case alone would not be enough
steps.stepSummary: If רב נחמן had taught only the valley case, we might think a house is different and is sold whole. So both cases are needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he had taught only about a valley, we would say: the seller had no way to mark off one field there. But a house could have been marked off, and he did not do it, so we might say he sold all of it. That is why both are needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its explanation of why רב נחמן taught two rulings. This is the second half of the argument started in step 12.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a בקעה, all the fields look alike, so the seller had no easy words to mark off one field; that excuses him. In a בית, he could have described the exact part he meant. Since he didn't, we might think he sold the whole building, so רב נחמן had to teach the house case too.

keyTerms.meaning: it is needed (both rulings are necessary)

steps.whatToRemember: רב נחמן taught both the house and the valley because each one alone could have led us to the wrong conclusion about the other.

phrases.english: And if he had taught us only the valley case,

phrases.aramaic: מִשּׁוּם דְּלָא הֲוָה לֵיהּ לְמִימְצַר לֵיהּ,
phrases.english: we would say it is because he had no way to mark its borders,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל בַּיִת – דַּהֲוָה לֵיהּ לְמִימְצַר לֵיהּ
phrases.english: but a house, where he did have a way to mark its borders
and he did not mark them,
he sold him all of it;
therefore it is needed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the two-sided explanation begun in step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The house case is needed because the residence could have been marked off, so failing to mark it might have meant the whole building was sold.

steps.title: Whose view does אביי's sale clause follow?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes אביי's advice that a seller should write 'I have not held back anything in this sale' and asks whose opinion this matches.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose view does this follow? רב מרי, son of שמואל's daughter, said in the name of אביי: someone who sells something must write for the buyer, 'I have not held back anything for myself in this sale.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a practical rule about writing a sale document and asks which opinion it is based on. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If every sale automatically included everything inside the borders, this sentence would not be needed. The fact that אביי says to write it suggests that, without it, a seller could claim he kept something back.

phrases.english: Whose view does this follow,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַב מָרִי בְּרֵיהּ דְּבַת שְׁמוּאֵל (בַּר שִׁילַת)
phrases.english: that Rav Mari, son of the daughter of Shmuel (bar Shilat), said
phrases.notes: Some versions have the words in round brackets and some leave them out.

phrases.english: in the name of Abaye:

phrases.aramaic: הַאי מַאן דִּמְזַבְּנִי לֵיהּ מִידֵּי לְחַבְרֵיהּ,
phrases.english: One who sells something to his friend
must write for him:
"I have not held back in this sale of mine
anything for myself"

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּמַאן אָזְלָא הָא דְּאָמַר רַב מָרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from explaining רב נחמן to finding a practical rule that depends on him.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which opinion is the basis for אביי's required clause?

steps.title: The clause follows רב נחמן
steps.stepSummary: אביי's clause matches רב נחמן in the name of רבה בר אבוה, who holds that a seller can keep part of what lies inside the borders.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose view? Like רב נחמן, who said in the name of רבה בר אבוה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers its own question: אביי's rule follows רב נחמן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן taught that naming borders does not automatically sell everything inside them. That is why a careful buyer needs the seller to write 'I held back nothing'; it closes the door on later claims.

keyTerms.meaning: the teacher in whose name רב נחמן spoke

steps.whyThisMatters: It turns רב נחמן's ruling into practical advice for writing a שטר מכירה.

phrases.english: Whose view?

phrases.aramaic: כְּרַב נַחְמָן אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ.
phrases.english: Like Rav Nachman, who said in the name of Rabba bar Avuh.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The clause is based on רב נחמן's view that a sale within borders may still leave parts unsold.

steps.title: A seller with two plots of the same name
steps.stepSummary: A man sold 'the land of בי חייא', but he owned two plots both called by that name. The question is whether both are sold.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain man said to his friend, 'I am selling you the land of בי חייא.' He had two plots of land that were both called 'of בי חייא.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a new story and sets up a problem. This step prepares for רב אשי's ruling in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The seller used a name that fits two different plots. The unspoken question is whether the name covers both plots or only one.

keyTerms.meaning: the family or estate of חייא, the name of the plots

phrases.english: There was a certain man who said to his friend:
"I am selling you the land of Bei Chiya."
He had two plots of land
that were called "of Bei Chiya."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new case about how sale wording is read.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does 'the land of בי חייא' include both plots with that name?

steps.title: רב אשי: only one plot is sold
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי rules that the seller said 'land' in the singular, so he sold only one plot.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: He told him one; he did not tell him two.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers the case: only one of the two plots goes to the buyer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The seller said ארעא, a singular word. A singular word means one plot, so the buyer cannot claim both.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
He told him one;
phrases.notes: He means the seller said 'land' as one word, not 'lands'.

phrases.english: he did not tell him two.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי חֲדָא אֲמַר לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the case set up in step 16.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A singular word sells only one plot.

steps.title: Saying 'lands' with no number means two
steps.stepSummary: If the seller says 'lands' without saying how many, he must give only two, the smallest number that counts as plural.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he told him 'lands' with no details, the smallest number of 'lands' is two.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues with a list of sale wordings. Here the seller used the plural word ארעתא without a number.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A plural means at least two, and we only hold the seller to the least the word must mean. So even if he owns many fields, he gives just two.

phrases.english: And if he told him "lands" with no details,
the smallest number of "lands" is two.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the singular 'land' to the plural 'lands'.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An unspecified plural 'lands' obligates only two plots.

steps.title: 'All lands' means all fields but not orchards
steps.stepSummary: If the seller says 'all lands', he sells every field he owns, but not his orchards and vineyards.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he told him 'all lands', it means all the lands he has, except orchards and vineyards.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the next wording: כל ארעתא, 'all lands'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'all' removes the limit of two, so every field is included. But orchards and vineyards are not called plain 'lands', so they stay with the seller.

phrases.english: And if he told him "all lands,"
it means all the lands that he has,
except for orchards and vineyards.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Widens the wording from 'lands' to 'all lands'.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'All lands' includes every field but excludes orchards and vineyards.

steps.title: 'זיהרא' includes orchards but not houses or slaves
steps.stepSummary: If the seller says 'זיהרא' (landed property), even orchards and vineyards are sold, but not houses and slaves.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he told him 'זיהרא', even orchards and vineyards are included, except houses and slaves.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the widest wording in the list, זיהרא, and says what it covers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: זיהרא is a broader word than 'lands', so it takes in orchards and vineyards too. Still, houses and slaves are not called זיהרא, so they are not sold.
steps.whatToRemember: Each wording reaches a little further: 'land' = one plot; 'lands' = two; 'all lands' = every field but not orchards; 'זיהרא' = orchards too, but not houses or slaves.

phrases.english: And if he told him "zihara,"
phrases.notes: זיהרא means landed property, a broader word than just 'lands'.

phrases.english: even orchards and vineyards are included,
except for houses and slaves.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Widens the wording one more level, beyond 'all lands'.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'זיהרא' includes orchards and vineyards but excludes houses and slaves.
